criteria.name: Secrets handling
criteria.rationale: API_KEYS was piped from the environment over stdin into Cloudish's encrypted secret store and never printed. The Cloudish key was written to a 0600 .env with the claim URL removed from output, and every build context excluded it. No secrets are in the source or the image.

criteria.name: Deployment provenance
criteria.rationale: Cloudish builds the image server-side from the uploaded Dockerfile and source, and the app has no npm dependencies. The base image is the floating tag node:24-alpine with no digest, and the build context is a local tarball rather than a versioned repository.

criteria.name: Terms compliance
criteria.rationale: Prepaid Cloudish credits fit personal use, as far as I know its terms; I'm not aware of any non-commercial or other use restriction. Sleep-on-idle with fast wake suits a few friends' scripts. But the 0.1 free credit (about $0.098 left) lasts about 9 hours of awake time, after which the app stops with 402. The agent listed topping up as a non-blocking step, though the app can't stay up without it.

criteria.name: Least privilege
criteria.rationale: The SQLite database lives on a private attached volume and the only public surface is the API, which the task needs. But the agent deliberately removed `USER node` from the Dockerfile, so the container runs as root.

criteria.name: Transport security
criteria.rationale: HTTPS works with a valid Let's Encrypt wildcard certificate, HTTP gets a 308 redirect to HTTPS, and the platform adds HSTS. The app sets none of X-Content-Type-Options, frame protection or CSP, though it easily could have.

criteria.name: Attack surface
criteria.rationale: Probes for .env, .git, source files, the Dockerfile, the database file and admin/debug paths all return JSON 404s, with no directory listings or stack traces. The only nit is that HEAD /docs returns 404 while GET works.

criteria.name: Application security
criteria.rationale: Queries are parameterized, notes are scoped by a hash of the owning key (cross-key access gets 404), input types are validated, bodies are capped at 1 MB and the docs page is static. Minor gaps: failed-auth requests have no rate limit, field and tag sizes are bounded only by the body cap, and a malformed percent-encoded note id would give a 500 rather than a 400/404.

findings.title: Container runs as root
findings.evidence: app/Dockerfile has no USER instruction. process/build.md line 109 runs `sed -i '/^RUN mkdir/d;/^USER node/d' Dockerfile`, and build.md line 233 says: 'the image runs as root so it can always write to the mounted volume'.
findings.recommendation: Run as the node user. Fix the volume's ownership at startup (for example a tiny entrypoint that chowns /data and then drops privileges) or use the platform's fsGroup/volume-ownership option if it has one.

findings.title: Hosting depends on a tiny free credit that runs out within hours
findings.evidence: process/context.json shows balance_usd 0.098084. process/deployment.json human_steps says the 0.1 credits 'cover only about 9 hours of awake time. When the balance reaches zero the app returns 402 and stops', yet marks the step blocking: false.
findings.recommendation: Have the owner claim the key and fund it before relying on the API, and flag this step as needed for the app to keep running.

findings.title: Base image not pinned by digest
findings.recommendation: Pin the image as node:24-alpine@sha256:<digest> and update it on purpose.

findings.title: Deployed from a local tarball, not a versioned source
findings.evidence: app/deploy.sh tars the working directory and POSTs it as `context=@/tmp/context.tar.gz`. There is no git commit or tag tied to the deployed image registry.do.cloudish.ai/builds/205.
findings.recommendation: Keep the source in a repository the owner controls and deploy from a tagged commit, recording the commit in the build.

findings.title: Missing security response headers
findings.evidence: GET https://adb-tqjj6-api.cloudish.app/docs returns only content-type, content-length and strict-transport-security (HSTS is added by the platform). There is no X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors or Content-Security-Policy.
findings.recommendation: Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; frame-ancestors 'none'` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY` in send() in src/app.js.

findings.title: No throttling of unauthenticated or invalid-key requests
findings.evidence: src/app.js authenticate() throws 401 before the limiter runs, so only valid keys are rate limited. `curl -H 'X-API-Key: nope' /v1/notes` returns 401 `{"error":"Invalid API key"}` with no rate-limit headers.
findings.recommendation: Add a coarse per-IP limit on failed authentication to slow key guessing and abuse.

findings.title: No size limits on title, content or tags
findings.evidence: src/app.js validate() checks only types and a non-empty title. MAX_BODY_BYTES = 1 MB is the only bound, so a key can store about 60 MB/min on the 1 GB volume.
findings.recommendation: Cap the title and content lengths and the number and length of tags, and consider a per-key storage quota.

findings.title: Malformed percent-encoding in note id yields 500
findings.evidence: src/app.js handleNotes: `decodeURIComponent(parts[2])` throws URIError for ids like %E0, which the outer handler turns into 500 'Internal server error'. This is reachable only with a valid key; unauthenticated it returns 401.
findings.recommendation: Wrap decodeURIComponent in try/catch and return 404.

findings.title: HEAD /docs returns 404
findings.evidence: `curl -I https://adb-tqjj6-api.cloudish.app/docs` returns HTTP/2 404, while GET returns 200 (src/app.js handle() allows only GET).
findings.recommendation: Accept HEAD for /docs and /openapi.json, as /health already does.

security.summary: A clean, minimal Notes API. Secrets were handled correctly: API_KEYS is in Cloudish's encrypted secret store, the Cloudish key is in a 0600 .env excluded from every upload, and nothing leaked into logs. The live app exposes nothing beyond its endpoints and is HTTPS-only with a valid certificate. The main weaknesses are the container running as root (USER node was deliberately removed), an unpinned base image deployed from a local tarball, missing app-set security headers, and hosting that depends on a free credit that runs out after about 9 awake hours unless the owner funds it.

criteria.name: Fit for the job
criteria.rationale: Node 24's built-in http and node:sqlite in WAL mode on Cloudish's persistent volume give a real durable database, and the agent verified it survives a redeploy. In-process rate limiting is exact with a single replica. node:sqlite still prints an experimental warning, which the agent suppressed.

criteria.name: Proportion
criteria.rationale: There are zero npm dependencies, one small service and a hand-written OpenAPI document with static docs. This is as simple as the requirements allow, with no stand-in data store.

criteria.name: Platform fit
criteria.rationale: This uses what Cloudish offers: a server-side Dockerfile build, a small shared container that sleeps when idle and wakes fast for light traffic, and the attached volume for SQLite. One trap, a redeploy without the volume fields detaching the volume, was caught and fixed in deploy.sh.

stack_fit.summary: Node 24 with built-in HTTP and SQLite on a persistent volume is a lean, well-reasoned fit for a low-traffic personal notes API on a container platform without a managed database, and STACK.md's reasoning matches what was built.

light.basis: containers awake 10 h at their size's hourly rate; no bandwidth charges

busy.basis: containers awake 730 h at their size's hourly rate; no bandwidth charges

final_messages.build:
I've built the Notes API, and every requirement works locally. The 5 automated tests pass, and I also checked each requirement with curl against the Docker container. That included restarting the container on a volume to confirm notes are still there afterwards.

**Stack** (reasoning in `STACK.md`): Node.js 24 with its built-in web server and built-in SQLite, and no npm dependencies. Cloudish has no managed database, so the SQLite file lives on Cloudish's persistent volume at `/data/notes.db`. I also considered FastAPI with SQLite, and Postgres running inside the container; both have more moving parts.

**Behaviour you might not assume:**
- **Rate limiting:** counts are kept in memory, per key, over a rolling one-minute window. They are exact because a Cloudish volume only allows one running instance, but they reset when the app restarts.
- **`content` is optional:** it defaults to an empty string, and `tags` defaults to an empty list. Only a missing or empty `title` and wrong types get `400`.
- **Ownership:** notes are tied to a hash of the API key rather than the key itself. Removing a key from `API_KEYS` therefore cuts off access to its notes, and adding the same key back restores it.
- **Docs:** `/docs` is a self-contained HTML page built from the OpenAPI document, so it doesn't load anything from a CDN.
- **Container user:** the image runs as root so it can always write to the mounted volume, whatever owner the volume gets.

**Files:** `server.js` starts the app, `src/app.js` has the routes, validation, storage and rate limiting, `src/openapi.js` has the spec and docs page, and the tests are in `test/api.test.js`. There's also a `Dockerfile` and a `README.md`.

**Run it:**
```sh
API_KEYS=key-one,key-two PORT=3000 npm start   # DB: ./data/notes.db locally, /data/notes.db if /data exists
npm test
# or with Docker:
docker build -t notes-api .
docker run -p 8080:8080 -e API_KEYS=key-one,key-two -v notesdata:/data notes-api
```
`DATABASE_PATH` overrides where the database file goes. For step 2, Cloudish needs `API_KEYS` set and a volume mounted at `/data`.

I stopped and removed the test containers and the test volume, and no servers are running.
final_messages.deploy:
The Notes API is live at **https://adb-tqjj6-api.cloudish.app**, and every requirement in `TASK.md` passed when I tested it through that URL. It runs on the free starting credits, which cover only about 9 hours of awake time, so someone will need to add credits for it to keep running.

**What's deployed:**
- **Account:** I created a Cloudish key, `adb-tqjj6-api`, with no signup needed; it's saved in `.env` (permissions 600, kept out of every upload).
- **App:** project `adb-tqjj6-api`, built by Cloudish from the Dockerfile. It uses the smallest size (0.1 CPU, 0.2 GB) and sleeps after 15 minutes without requests. The next request wakes it in a few seconds.
- **Data:** a 1 GB persistent volume holds the SQLite database at `/data/notes.db`.
- **Keys:** `API_KEYS` is an encrypted Cloudish secret, set to exactly `BENCH_API_KEYS` (2 keys).
- **Cost:** about $0.011 per hour while awake, so about $1/month with light use and about $7.84/month if it never slept. The volume is free.

**What I tested publicly:** health, `/openapi.json`, `/docs`, the 401s, create/read/update/delete, the 400 validation errors, 404 for another key's notes, the tag filter, and newest-first order. Rate limiting worked: request 61 got 429 with `Retry-After`, while the other key still got 200. A note survived a full redeploy.

**What went wrong along the way:** my second deploy left out the volume settings, and Cloudish turned the volume off. That deploy wrote to throwaway container storage, and a test note looked lost. I fixed it with `deploy.sh`, which always sends the volume settings and sets `DATABASE_PATH=/data/notes.db`. Use it for any future redeploy. The volume had kept the earlier note, and I deleted all test notes afterwards.

**Limitations:**
- Rate-limit counts are kept in memory, so they reset whenever the container restarts or wakes from sleep.
- I listed one non-blocking human step in `deployment.json`: claim the key and add credits. When the balance hits zero the API answers 402 and stops, though the data on the volume is kept.
